answer: Genocide is a legal term. The 1948 Genocide Convention defines it as certain acts committed with intent to destroy a national, ethnic, racial or religious group, in whole or in part. In January 2024 the International Court of Justice ordered Israel to take measures to prevent such acts and did not order a ceasefire. It found plausible the Palestinians' right to be protected from genocide; its then-president later said, according to press reports of one BBC interview, that it did not decide that the genocide claim itself was plausible. When intent has to be inferred from conduct, the ICJ has held it must be the only reasonable inference, and scholars disagree whether that is met in Gaza. Amnesty International (December 2024) and a UN commission of inquiry (September 2025) concluded that Israel committed genocide. Israel and the US reject this. The court has not ruled on the merits.

facts.text: When genocidal intent has to be inferred from a pattern of conduct, the ICJ has held (in Croatia v. Serbia, repeating Bosnia v. Serbia) that it must be the only inference that could reasonably be drawn from the acts. The Commission of Inquiry says it applied this test, and says other aims, such as a military advantage, do not rule out genocidal intent as long as it is the only reasonable inference.

not_claimed: This card does not say whether Israel is or is not committing genocide. It says what the word legally requires and where the case stands.
It does not say the ICJ found genocide, and it does not say the ICJ rejected the claim.
It does not say that Amnesty or the UN Commission are wrong, or that Israel's rejection is right.
It does not say anything about whether Israel's military actions are lawful in other respects; war-crimes questions are separate from the genocide question.
could_not_verify: The ICJ's Bosnia v. Serbia and Croatia v. Serbia judgments could not be fetched; the 'only reasonable inference' standard is cited from the Commission's report (which quotes both), Legal Tribune Online and the Notre Dame piece.
I found Stefan Talmon's view only as reported by LTO, not in Der Spiegel itself.
The Israeli government's own statements (foreign ministry post, the written pleadings) were not read at source; Israel's replies are cited through the ICJ order and news reports.

Fact 4 (Joan Donoghue's explanation of 'plausible') is marked short: it is one BBC HARDtalk interview, which I could not read or hear, reported by the Jerusalem Post, JNS and Joshua Rozenberg's page (which is partly paywalled). I looked for a transcript, the BBC's own page, and the same explanation in her own written words, and found none. The answer attributes it to press reports of the interview.

Fact 13: the ICJ's own case page lists the order of 21 May 2026 fixing time-limits, but the order's text could not be fetched, so the dates (reply 22 November 2027, rejoinder 22 May 2029) come from The Citizen, Mail & Guardian and JNS, which report the same order, with the South African Presidency as a government voice.

answer_claims.says: The 1948 Genocide Convention defines it as certain acts committed with intent to destroy a national, ethnic, racial or religious group, in whole or in part.
In January 2024 the International Court of Justice ordered Israel to take measures to prevent such acts and did not order a ceasefire.

It found plausible the Palestinians' right to be protected from genocide; its then-president later said, according to press reports of one BBC interview, that it did not decide that the genocide claim itself was plausible.
When intent has to be inferred from conduct, the ICJ has held it must be the only reasonable inference, and scholars disagree whether that is met in Gaza.
Amnesty International (December 2024) and a UN commission of inquiry (September 2025) concluded that Israel committed genocide.
Israel and the US reject this.
The court has not ruled on the merits.

skeptic.notes: Round 3: checked what changed. Fact 13: the ICJ case page (case 192) lists 'Order of 21 May 2026 fixing of time-limits: reply and rejoinder' and no judgment on the merits; the dates 22 Nov 2027 and 22 May 2029 come from three outlets and the Presidency, not from the page itself, which gives only the title: acceptable, with that stated here. Fact 4 (Donoghue): reworded by me to what the sources are, press reports of one BBC interview, and the answer now says 'according to press reports of one BBC interview'; JPost and JNS quote her directly, the Rozenberg page is paywalled to a headline; the interview was not read. Fact 7 checked: Notre Dame cites Bosnia v. Serbia para 373 and Croatia v. Serbia paras 146-148, so with the Commission report (quoting Croatia) and LTO it is three readers of the ICJ's holding, though the Notre Dame quote chosen is weak [nit: replace with the para 373 sentence]. Strongest objection from critics of Israel: the officials' statements the ICJ itself noted are in contested only, not a fact [should-fix]. From defenders: the Commission's method is disputed by EJIL's author and Israel did not take part, in facts 10 and contested; the criticism of its method is not a fact [should-fix]. Neither makes the answer misleading; every opposing finding is stated at full strength. No 'Our reading' sentence; the answer states no conclusion of the authors, consistent with docs/chapters.md.
